newsitem.title: BRAZIL: FOCUS-Brazil still haunted by hyper-inflation past.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Brazil still haunted by hyper-inflation past.

text.p: Just when Brazil thought it had pulled all its fiscal skeletons from the closet, a new high court ruling threatens to slap an unexpected $20 billion on to an already bloated federal payroll.
Brazil watchers say the ruling in favor of a retroactive civil service pay hike is a sobering reminder that the nation is not yet free of its hyper-inflation past.
It also highlights the vulnerability of the government's bid to put Latin America's largest economy on a sure footing after years of financial mismanagement.
"The government is extremely worried about the ghost of Christmas past in terms of indexing for inflation," said David Fleischer, a political analyst based in Brasilia.
"This is one of those nasty inheritances from previous administrations that they now have to deal with," Fleischer said.

After owning up late last year to what could amount to a $50 billion shortfall in a federal housing fund, Finance Minister Pedro Malan triumphantly declared that Brazil had buried its final fiscal skeleton.

But Wednesday's ruling by the Supreme Federal Tribunal -- which was limited to just 11 workers -- was expected to encourage up to one million past and present federal workers to sue for an estimated $20 billion in backpay.
Most legal experts think the workers will get the money, which will make it increasingly hard for Brasilia to rein in federal spending -- considered the government's chief challenge.
Although the fiscal impact will be great, some observers say the possible political ramifications are even more worrisome.

First, the high court's 6-4 vote startled the government and the markets because the court has normally sided with Brasilia in inflation-related cases. In fact, prior to this week's ruling, the court had been seen as an ally of the government in its drive to reform the Brazilian economy.

"There is a political side to this ruling that may be even more important than the fiscal issue which is that the civil service may now see the court as an ally in their fight to block civil service and pension reform," said Mauro Schneider, chief economist at ING Barings in Brazil.

Pension and civil service reform are the two pillars of President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's bid to reform Brazil's federal finances. Both reforms, which must take the form of constitutional amendments, would allow the government to fire workers and cut benefits.
Cardoso proved last month that he had the political muscle to force a controversial bill allowing his re-election past an obstinate Congress.
But analysts say his new-found political clout may get him nowhere with the supreme court, which is almost certain to rule on the constitutionality of both pension and civil service reforms.
"Cardoso emerged from last month's re-election vote as a kind of Superman. But now he has encountered some kryptonite in the supreme court," Fleischer said.
